questions.question: What probability reversal defines the prosecutor's fallacy?
options: Using Bayes' rule with an explicit partition of cases.
Subtracting an overlap term in inclusion-exclusion.

questions.question: Which two probabilities are confused in the prosecutor's fallacy?
What does the prosecutor's fallacy do to evidence?
options: It proves the hypothesis is false
It can make evidence sound stronger than it is.

questions.question: Which rule shows why posterior probabilities require more than a likelihood?
options: The definition of a sample outcome

questions.question: What else is needed besides rare evidence to assess a hypothesis?
options: Only the number of letters in the hypothesis
A guarantee that all events are disjoint

questions.question: Which statement is an example of the prosecutor's fallacy?
options: Counting cards in a poker hand
Equating $P(E\mid H)$ with $P(H\mid E)$ via a rare DNA match.
Checking whether two events are disjoint.

questions.question: A disease test is rare-positive among healthy people. Which probability is not automatically the disease probability?
options: The probability of disease given a positive result
The probability of the whole sample space
The probability of a positive result given no disease
The probability of disease or no disease

questions.question: In fraud detection, why is a suspicious transaction pattern not automatically decisive?
options: Suspicious patterns can never be evidence.
Compare it under fraud and non-fraud explanations.

questions.question: If $P(E\mid H)=0.001$, what conclusion is fallacious without more information?
Which expression is the posterior probability of a hypothesis after evidence?
Why can rare evidence fail to be decisive?
options: Rare evidence always has probability one
It may occur under competing hypotheses or small priors.

questions.question: What is the conditional-probability error at the heart of the fallacy?
options: Reversing the condition and the event

questions.question: How does prevalence matter in medical-test reasoning?
options: Prior disease probability, affecting the posterior.
It is irrelevant once sensitivity is high.
It is the same as the false-positive rate

questions.question: A lab says $P(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})$ is tiny. Which probability is still not directly known?
A test has high sensitivity, but the disease is extremely rare. What caution follows?
options: The disease probability after a positive result must be one
A positive result may still have a low positive predictive value

questions.question: A suspicious transaction pattern occurs in $1\%$ of legitimate transactions. Why is this not enough to conclude fraud?
options: We also need the fraud base rate and the pattern probability under fraud
The pattern is not an event
The $1\%$ figure is already the probability of fraud given the pattern

questions.question: Why is the name 'inverse fallacy' appropriate?
options: It computes complements instead of intersections.
It counts permutations in reverse order

questions.question: What correction does Bayes' rule add to the prosecutor's fallacy?
options: It treats a rare match probability as the guilt probability directly.
It ignores base rates once a piece of evidence is observed.
It combines likelihoods with priors and competing evidence probabilities.
It makes the false-positive probability equal to zero.

questions.question: Suppose $P(E\mid H)=0.99$ and $P(H)=0.001$. Why can $P(H\mid E)$ still be small?
options: A high likelihood always makes the posterior $0.99$.
The evidence probability must be zero
The prior of $H$ is tiny and alternatives may also yield $E$.

questions.question: A report says a code collision is rare for a random person. What extra comparison is needed before blaming a specific person?
options: Only the number of digits in the code
Only whether the event has a complement
Whether two sets form a partition of books.
